articles.title: Musk opens the door to a SpaceX-Tesla merger as shareholders weigh a deal
articles.summary: Elon Musk's rocket and AI company posted net income of $4.4 billion for the July-September period (Kent NISHIMURA) Elon Musk said Tuesday he would back a merger of SpaceX and Tesla, as his rocket and AI company reported its first quarterly profit since going public, driven by deals to rent out computing power to AI firms. Asked about a possible tie-up on a call with analysts, Musk said he felt he was "tap dancing through a minefield," but that a combination would be "a good idea." Shares in SpaceX shot up nearly five percent in after-hours trading following the comments. Musk said special committees of independent directors at both SpaceX and Tesla have been set up to study the idea at the request of shareholders. He added that he could not take part in their talks because he has a conflict of interest. Musk is chief executive of both companies, and also serves as chairman and chief technology officer of SpaceX. He owned 48.4 percent of SpaceX as of June 30, according to a regulatory filing, and controls more than 82 percent of its voting power through super-voting shares. He holds about 20 percent of Tesla. The committees have not agreed on the terms of any deal and there is no guarantee they will, Musk said, cautioning that it would be overstating it to treat a merger as a certainty. Any deal would need the backing of a majority of all Tesla shares, not just those cast in a vote, which Musk called "quite a high hurdle." He said the two companies could gain from working together on AI software, chip design, robotics and space-based computing. His remarks came after SpaceX posted net income of $4.4 billion for the July-September period, compared with a loss of $1.1 billion a year earlier. Revenue jumped 161 percent to $14.6 billion. The quarterly results follow a bumpy start on Wall Street. SpaceX began trading on the Nasdaq on June 12 after an IPO priced at $135 a share that raised about $85.7 billion. Its first earnings report as a listed company showed second-quarter revenue of $7.8 billion and a net loss of $541 million. The AI division, which SpaceX now calls "Super Intelligence," drove the turnaround. Super Intelligence is US President Donald Trump's preferred term for AI. The unit's revenue rose more than nine times from a year earlier to $7.6 billion, overtaking the Starlink satellite internet business as the company's largest source of sales. - Cloud computing - SpaceX credited new cloud services agreements, wider adoption of its Grok chatbot and its acquisition of Cursor, an artificial intelligence coding startup. SpaceX’s cloud customers include Anthropic, which agreed in May to pay nearly $45 billion over three years for computing power at SpaceX's Colossus data centers. Google signed on in June, agreeing to pay $920 million a month from October through June 2029. The AI unit turned an operating profit of $431 million, compared with a loss of $1.7 billion a year earlier. As with other AI companies, spending remains heavy. SpaceX invested $19.6 billion in the quarter, $16.4 billion of it in AI, bringing capital spending for the first nine months of the year to $48 billion. Its computing capacity reached 1.7 gigawatts, up from 0.6 gigawatts a year earlier. Musk said he was "fairly confident" SpaceX could bring an additional 10 gigawatts of computing capacity online in 2027. That would come on top of the roughly 2.5 to 3.0 gigawatts it expects to have running by the end of this year. He added that power, cooling and electrical equipment were "somewhat of a limiting factor." Revenue at the Starlink satellite internet unit grew 69 percent to $5.2 billion, and consumer subscribers reached 13.6 million. Average monthly revenue per consumer, however, fell to $69 from $83 a year earlier. SpaceX also completed the first revenue-generating flight of Starship, the giant rocket central to Musk's Mars ambitions and to deploying satellites at scale. The flight carried 26 next-generation Starlink satellites into orbit. arp/mlm This article originally appeared on AFP at https://finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles/musk-says-backs-spacex-tesla-220507985.html

articles.title: Trump unveils fraud whistleblower rewards, but he gets to decide who gets paid
articles.summary: Washington — President Trump on Tuesday announced the federal government will compensate whistleblowers who report people defrauding the U.S. government and taxpayers, but said he will decide who gets paid. "I will be the arbitrator of all of these decisions," the president said during his Oval Office announcement with Vice President JD Vance, who heads up the administration's fraud task force, beside him. "In other words, I'll determine whether or not the person is deserving and I'll determine — and I will be very generous, believe me." Through the Fraud Whistleblower Incentive Program, Mr. Trump said whistleblowers, who can be ordinary citizens, will be eligible to receive 1% of the amount of fraud they report, even if the reported fraud is $100 billion. America.gov/fraud , however, says successful whistleblowers will be paid up to $30,000, dependent upon the report resulting in criminal charges. Asked by CBS News for clarification, Mr. Trump said there is no limit to whistleblower compensation, and criminal charges aren't necessary. "That's the answer. I quit while I'm ahead," Vance joked. The president promised to be "fair" in his decisions. "You'll get your money immediately, but I'll make the determination," he continued. "So if two people are fighting over it, maybe they'll split it or maybe whatever, but I'll make that determination." The America.gov/fraud website says reports are encrypted and will go directly to the Treasury Department. It's not immediately clear who reviews reports, although the Department of Justice will administer the program. The first person to benefit from the program is Nick Shirley , a 20-something YouTuber who published a video alleging fraud at childcare centers in Minnesota. He stood alongside Mr. Trump in the Oval Office Tuesday and was presented with a $10,000 check. Some whistleblowers can already receive compensation from the False Claims Act, which allows some whistleblowers to be entitled to up to 25% to 30% of proceeds recovered. But the requirements are stringent. Vance said "99%" of the fraud they're finding isn't covered by the False Claims Act. Naomi Seligman, president of nonprofit Whistleblower Aid, was skeptical of Mr. Trump's announcement, saying the president "is more interested in hunting down whistleblowers." "If the president is truly interested in rooting out wrongdoing, Whistleblower Aid invites him to start by examining the violations perpetrated by his own administration, including senior officials," she said in a statement. "We would happily work with him on this vital accountability effort to help save our democracy." articles.title: Trump says Russia 'has been fine on Ukraine' as he makes deals with Putin
articles.summary: A series of Trump administration moves over the last two weeks — including decisions to lift sanctions on Russian diesel and delay other measures targeting the Russian economy — have led both Republicans and Democrats to question whether President Trump is changing course and siding with Russian President Vladimir Putin over Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in the war between their two countries. "Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine," Trump told reporters on Monday. "They haven't been doing much." In contrast, the president continued, "We've given a lot to Ukraine. They've given nothing to us. Remember that." Russia and Ukraine have been at war for more than 12 years. But in February 2022, the conflict entered a new, deadlier phase when Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine and tried to seize territory. The fighting has since become a grinding war of attrition. The United States has generally supported Ukraine, even as direct military aid has waned during Trump's second term . The administration's latest steps, however, "amount to a major reversal in U.S. strategy," the New York Times reported on Sunday . "The breach with Ukraine has been sudden and perhaps irreparable." So what's going on here? Posting Sunday on social media , Trump defended his actions by insisting that he is "in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine" and doesn't "want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table." Ukraine, he said, is targeting diesel refineries in Russia, which is "hurting the world diesel markets, including those in the United States." He said that "farmers, ranchers, and businesses of all kinds are suffering greatly from this, but Russia is, nevertheless, sending, at a low price, millions of barrels of diesel to the World." But even Republicans have pushed back. "I think it's clear Russia is the aggressor, and we've got to do everything we can to put economic pressure on Russia," GOP Sen. Rick Scott of Florida told the Associated Press over the weekend. "So it's not the first thing I would be doing." When Zelensky was asked last week if he believed Ukraine was "losing" the U.S., he replied: "Yes." "It's painful when President Trump chooses one ‌side, not our ⁠side," Zelensky said. On Tuesday, Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff met with Zelensky in Oslo , Norway. Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, participated via video link. On Wednesday, Witkoff and Kushner will reportedly fly to St. Petersburg, Russia, to meet Putin in his hometown with "an updated set of [peace] proposals," according to the BBC. Is a diplomatic breakthrough in the offing? Here's what you need to know about the latest developments. What's changed in recent days Oct. 9: Trump said he had reached an agreement with Putin to supply diesel to the U.S. and global markets. Minutes later, the Treasury Department announced that it would be lifting sanctions on Russian diesel exports through April 2027. Those sanctions — which limited Putin's ability to bankroll the invasion of Ukraine — have been in place since 2022. "Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!" the president wrote on social media. Oct. 10: Trump blamed Zelensky for high U.S. diesel prices and said Ukraine should replace him. "He wants to make problems for the world. He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel," Trump told reporters before leaving for a campaign rally in Tennessee . "I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals and for some reason he never does." Oct. 11: On social media, Trump declared an "ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine." He claimed that "both parties have agreed." Zelensky said the agreement was news to him , but added that he would be willing to pause attacks on Russian oil refineries if Russia pauses attacks on Ukraine's electrical grid and other energy infrastructure in return. Oct. 11-14: For three days, Zelensky held his fire on Russian oil refineries. Meanwhile, Putin continued to bombard Ukraine's energy infrastructure, leaving hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians without power ahead of winter. The Trump administration clarified that its "energy ceasefire" applied solely to attacks on oil refineries , but Ukraine doesn't have any fully operational oil refineries — Russia has repeatedly attacked and disabled the last one in recent years. Oct. 14: Ukraine discovered that its access to Elon Musk's Starlink satellite communications network — as well as Starshield, its military-grade counterpart — had been throttled , limiting its ability to defend itself from Russian ballistic missile attacks on energy infrastructure. "Right at the moment Trump was warning Zelensky not to attack Russian refineries, the Starshield settings were somehow altered, such that the system could not track objects traveling at speeds greater than about 100 miles per hour — woefully inadequate to detect Russian aerial assaults," the National Review explained . Citing four sources familiar with the discussions, the Telegraph reported that "Elon Musk approached Donald Trump with the idea of slowing down Starlink in Ukraine" and that Trump "agreed." In response, Trump denied any involvement, saying, "I don't know if it was anybody, but it wasn't me, and I don't think it was Elon." Musk wrote on social media that "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS." Reuters also reported that the "order to limit Starshield for Ukraine came from inside [the] White House." The Wall Street Journal reported this week that “Elon Musk ordered the slowdown” — “a decision that sparked panic in Kyiv and confusion inside the Trump administration.” Oct. 15: Zelensky said that Ukraine would resume attacking Russian oil refineries. "That's it," Zelensky told the Financial Times . "The block is out. We're done." Oct. 16: Trump issued an executive order waiving new sanctions against Russia — as well as tariffs on major buyers of Russian energy — that would have taken effect under the bipartisan Graham Act that he signed in September. "I'm not a big fan of Zelensky," Trump told Newsmax . "I find Zelensky to be more difficult to deal with than Putin." Oct. 18: Trump wrote on social media that his "decision on Russia is a very simple one" aimed at striking a peace deal and lowering energy costs for Americans. "Great progress is being made, and that includes current hostage negotiations," Trump claimed, saying that he doesn't  "want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table." He continued, "Russia is doing very little, if anything, to help the Islamic Republic of Iran, compared to what they could be doing, and I want to keep it that way, and will, unless stupid people get in the way." In contrast, Trump claimed Zelensky "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did." Oct. 19: Citing "a U.S. official and three additional people familiar with the situation," the Washington Post reported that the Trump administration is holding up "the transfer of interceptor missiles to Ukraine that are needed to protect the country from Russian missile and drone attacks." Around the same time, Trump criticized Zelensky again, saying, "It's time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine." Oct. 20: Witkoff and Kushner met with Zelensky in Oslo. According to the BBC , Zelensky suggested after the meeting that "crucial issues of early warning of Russia's ballistic missile strikes had… been resolved." Zelensky also said that he discussed Ukraine's access to missiles and Starlink with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio — and he expected "good results." Will Trump's deals with Putin lower U.S. diesel prices? Trump has accused Zelensky of "knowing that these attacks" on Russian refineries "are seriously hurting the world diesel markets, including those in the United States." It's true that the price of diesel is up about 77% so far this year — putting it near record highs and raising costs for American farmers, truckers and businesses (which in turn puts upward pressure on the price of consumer goods and services). But energy analysts say the Iran War, not Ukrainian attacks on Russia, is the major reason diesel is so much more expensive than it used to be. "The main issue is still the Strait of Hormuz, that there is not enough diesel coming out of the Strait of Hormuz," one recently told the New York Times . In 2025, Russian diesel exports accounted for roughly 9% of the global diesel trade — or about 700,000 barrels a day, according to S&P Global Energy. That number has fallen to about 140,000 barrels a day since Ukraine started targeting Russian oil refineries. Trump's deal with Putin would amount to another 75,000 barrels a day, according to the New York Times . That's not nothing — but experts say it's also not enough to make a huge price difference in the U.S. To put those 75,000 barrels in perspective, diesel exports from Saudi Arabia and other Middle Eastern countries have fallen by 800,000 barrels per day since the start of the Iran war in February. Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, estimated in an Oct. 9 social media post that Trump's deal with Russia could eventually lower the cost of diesel by 10 to 20 cents per gallon. Ryan Sweet, chief global economist at Oxford Economics, likened the impact to "putting a Band-Aid on a gunshot wound." And that's assuming Russia can deliver. According to the Times, "many analysts consider [even] those numbers to be unrealistic because roughly 40 to 50 percent of Russian refining capacity is offline" — and "repairing and restarting refineries can take months or years in the best of circumstances." Trump has been taking various steps to try to lower U.S. gas prices ahead of November's midterm elections, including signing an executive order allowing tax-free purchases of red-dyed off-road diesel. But an October AP poll found that only 17% of U.S. adults approve of how the president is handling the cost of living — and 65% now blame his policies for persistently high prices more than factors beyond his control. Will Trump's deals with Putin end the war? On Sunday, Energy Secretary Chris Wright described Trump's diesel deal as a "carrot" to get Russia to ease its assault on Ukraine. It's an "incentive to Russia, that if they can reduce the conflict with Ukraine, they can get an energy ceasefire or reduce the conflict such that they have diesel to export, we'll allow it to flow to world markets," Wright told ABC News . The Times has also reported that the "Trump administration's talks with Russia about ending the war in Ukraine have expanded to include a multibillion-dollar oil deal that would benefit Middle Eastern business executives with ties to the two main U.S. negotiators, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner." "The deal, which is contingent on approval from the U.S. government and the Kremlin, is for a sprawling set of oil fields, refineries and gas stations around the world owned by Lukoil, one of Russia's biggest energy companies," the paper added. Meanwhile, at their talks in Oslo on Tuesday, Witkoff and Kushner were expected to tell Zelensky that "holding out to retain occupied portions of the country's eastern provinces is not worth it — and that there is money to be made for Ukraine, as well, if it would only drop its objections to an accord, even one written largely on Russia's terms," according to the Times . In short, the Trump administration appears to be pushing harder than ever before to force Ukraine to cede sovereign territory to Russia as part of a negotiated end to the war. Whether Zelensky succumbs to that pressure remains to be seen. "I believe steps have been taken to convince Ukraine to capitulate," he told Bloomberg in an interview published on Sunday . "I don't want to think that our American partners believe the war could be ended sooner at Ukraine's expense. But that's how it looks." "If the United States will support Putin — it's unbelievable, it's a tragedy," Zelensky added Sunday on NBC News's Meet the Press . "If these two countries will be together, of course we will not prevail. And we will not be able to stand." articles.title: Zelensky welcomes renewed U.S. intelligence sharing as Russian attacks continue
articles.summary: Watch: Zelensky says US military intelligence sharing "works now" Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has said US intelligence sharing on deadly Russian missile attacks "works now" after talks with President Donald Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff. The meeting in Oslo came after accusations by Kyiv that Washington was withholding key intelligence - a claim rejected as "scandalous" by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Finnish President Alexander Stubb, who also took part in the talks, said "genuine progress" was made on proposals to achieve peace but gave no details and warned that patience would be needed. Zelensky and his European allies said it was now up to Russia to respond to the proposals agreed in Oslo when Witkoff arrives in St Petersburg on Wednesday. Witkoff was not present at the joint press conference after Tuesday's talks in the Norwegian capital. Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, another key envoy, took part in the meeting via video link. A US official later described the talks as "very productive and constructive", saying there was a "strong alignment at the working level" among the US, Ukraine and Europe on "the next steps". The official confirmed that Witkoff is due to meet President Vladimir Putin in Russia tomorrow to discuss the proposals and that Kushner will again participate virtually. Putin is yet to publicly comment on the latest developments, but Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov earlier said the Kremlin would listen to what Wiktoff would offer, while ruling out "any political concessions". Relations between Ukraine and the US have soured in recent weeks to the extent that Trump has said it is time for Ukraine to get a new president, and most recently "for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine". Ahead of next month's US midterm elections, Trump has also sought to blame Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries for fuel prices which have been rising since the start of the US-led war on Iran. Speaking after Zelensky's news conference in Oslo, Trump again told reporters at the White House he wanted Kyiv to "make a deal". He said Russia would like to "get it done" and it was "time for Ukraine to end this war". Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory. Russian drone attacks continued on Tuesday. Ukrainian officials said at least 10 people were killed - four in Kyiv and the capital region, another four in the eastern Donetsk region, and two in the central city of Dnipro. Trump and Zelensky appear at loggerheads despite Oslo optimism Ukrainians dying because US restricting intelligence sharing, Zelensky adviser tells BBC Trump envoy Witkoff (L) joined Finnish President Stubb (C) and Zelensky (R) before their talks in Oslo [Reuters] Addressing the issue of US intelligence sharing after Tuesday's talks, Zelensky said he was "thankful that intelligence works now". "Speaking about early warning, which is very important for our people, our children, adults, civilians because we can hear when ballistic[s] is coming - so we are thankful to American side, now it works, it's great," the Ukrainian president said. He said he also hoped for a good result on SpaceX's Starlink satellite access as well, after Ukraine's military had reported in recent days speed restrictions on the US platform used by Kyiv to carry out drone strikes against Russia. Before the Oslo talks, Zelensky said he had had a "constructive discussion" with Rubio about the need for US early warnings, missile interceptors and Starlink. Last week, a bipartisan group of US senators called for an urgent investigation into speed restrictions to the Starlink network in Ukraine. And Zelensky also restated that Ukraine was "ready for negotiations" to end the war. "Of course, we are not losing this war, but we are losing people because Russia attacks," he said. The Ukrainian leader added that "strong" security guarantees for Ukraine were also discussed in Oslo, as well as energy ceasefire proposals. Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, who also took part in the talks, stressed that Europe "needs to be at the table" during any discussions about how to end the Russia-Ukraine war. Unconfirmed reports earlier on Tuesday said the transfer of more US-made Patriot interceptor missiles - the only effective weapon in shooting down Russian ballistic missiles - had not yet been approved. Rubio, who is currently on a visit to India, admitted to reporters that it may be true that Patriot interceptors had not yet arrived in Ukraine - but he stressed that nothing had been denied to Kyiv intentionally. European leaders meanwhile have expressed concern about recent US statements from the US towards Russia. On Monday, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz spoke of "mixed pictures and messages" on the war, adding that he was trying to convince the American government "in total that this is something we have to resolve jointly". "It's really a big effort for our budgets, it's really a big thing for the European Union, but we are doing that and we are trying to keep on doing that until this terrible war ends," the German leader told Bloomberg TV. Asked during an interview on Monday whether or not he saw Ukraine as a US ally, US Vice-President JD Vance said Kyiv was "certainly a partner in some ways, but we have some divergent interests from time to time, like for example... I think they should stop bombing Russian energy". "We don't have a formal alliance as far as I know with Ukraine. They're not in Nato, I don't think they should be in Nato... we're gonna work together on some things, but also we're going to be opposite on some things too," he said. articles.title: U.S. is reportedly nearing a deal with Russia to free multiple jailed Americans
articles.summary: The Trump administration is closing in on a deal with Moscow that would see multiple Americans released from detention in Russia, two U.S. officials and another source familiar with the matter tell ABC News. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff and President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner have been leading the negotiations, which are said to be in the final stages, according to the sources. With Gilman's release from Russia, families of other detained Americans hope their relatives will be next They add that the talks have centered on freeing Stephen Hubbard , a 72-year-old retired teacher who is the only American held in Russia officially designated as wrongfully detained by the State Department, as well as several other U.S. citizens held by Moscow on what the administration said it believes are dubious charges. Moscow City Court Press Service via AP - PHOTO: In this Oct. 7, 2024, file photo released by the Moscow City Court Press Service, Stephen Hubbard, a U.S. citizen accused of fighting as a mercenary in Ukraine against Russia stands in a glass cage during a court session in Moscow. However, officials caution that while the terms of the arrangement are coming into focus, nothing has been finalized and it’s still possible it won’t materialize or that its scope will change. Asked about a potential deal to free Hubbard on Tuesday, Trump said he has spoken with Russian President Vladimir Putin about it "at length" and called for Hubbard's return to the U.S. "I've been talking to President Putin about Mr. Hubbard. I've been talking to him at length. I've asked him to release him. Let's see what happens. OK, let's see what happens. I'd love to get him back. It's time. It's time to have Mr. Hubbard back," Trump said in the Oval Office. News of the potential deal comes as Witkoff is expected to present Putin with a proposal for a partial ceasefire covering energy and food infrastructure, Finnish President Alexander Stubb said Tuesday. Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre joined Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky at a news briefing in Oslo, Norway, following talks with Witkoff. On Monday, Trump spoke about his dealings with Russia, saying he was "trying to get a hostage that the country has been after for a long time," presumably referring to Hubbard. "Let's see what happens," Trump said. "That'll be soon." Trump signs order waiving Graham Act sanctions on Russia, drawing backlash from some lawmakers and Zelenskyy On Tuesday, Russia's Deputy Foreign Minister Sergey Ryabkov was asked about a potential prisoner exchange between Russia and the U.S. "Dialogue on all these issues is ongoing through intelligence service channels," he said. Ryabkov added that Hubbard's name was "certainly familiar," but said he had "nothing to report" on the matter. Fabrice Coffrini/AFP via Getty Images, FILE - PHOTO: In this Jan. 10, 2022, file photo, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov looks on during a press conference following talks with US counterpart on soaring tensions over Ukraine, in Geneva. The White House declined to comment on the matter. It's not clear what Russia might receive in exchange for releasing U.S. citizens. However, Trump has made multiple policy decisions viewed as favorable to Moscow in recent days, including waiving newly imposed sanctions targeting Russian officials and oligarchs mandated by a bill Trump signed into law last month after it passed by wide margins in Congress. Trump has also increased pressure on Ukraine to halt attacks on Russian energy sites. There are currently at least eight American citizens and two dual U.S.-Russia nationals detained by Moscow: Hubbard, Gordon Black, Michael Leake, Robert Woodland, David Barnes, Daniel Schneider, Andre Khachatorrian, Chuck Zimmerman, Alexsandor Antonov and Eugene Spector. Families of the incarcerated Americans in Russia have called for the State Department to extend more wrongful detention designations, with Leake's family renewing its request in a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, saying Leake was "left behind" in the Aug. 1, 2024, prisoner trade. articles.title: Trump administration freezes another $1.2 billion in California Medicaid payments
articles.summary: Dr. Mehmet Oz, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services administrator, speaks Tuesday in the Oval Office as President Trump and Nick Shirley listen. (Jacquelyn Martin / Associated Press) The Trump administration is deferring an additional $1.2 billion in Medicaid reimbursements to California, citing concerns about potential fraud in a state program that helps older adults and people with disabilities with everyday tasks. Dr. Mehmet Oz, the administrator for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, said federal officials took action after they grew concerned about the rapid expansion of California’s personal care services program in recent years. State officials were notified of the decision Tuesday, he said. “California has been growing that program 24% in the last three years. That is twice the rate of every other state average in the country,” Oz said. “Impossible for us to understand how that could be so we are taking major action in California.” Oz did not provide any evidence of fraud but suggested the state was paying people too much taxpayer money to help with services that could be offered for free, like “paying somebody to carry groceries upstairs for your mom.” “Many of you would carry groceries upstairs for your mom for free, but in California, they will pay you a lot of money for it,” he said. Read more: Vance says $1.3 billion in Medicaid payments to California will be deferred over fraud concerns The move is the latest in a series of efforts by the administration to withhold federal money from California. In May, the administration held back $1.3 billion in Medicaid reimbursements to the state over concerns about “fraudsters” in the state’s hospice and in-home care programs. The actions have been part of a broad effort by the administration to rein in fraud in federal healthcare benefits programs, particularly in Democrat-led states. Democratic Sen. Alex Padilla criticized the administration’s decision. “This Administration’s track record speaks for itself: Fewer people have health insurance, premiums are up, and drug costs are higher. This decision will hurt older Californians, people with disabilities, and those recovering from illness or injury,” Padilla said in a statement. “The American people deserve better, and I’ll keep fighting against their attacks.” Gov. Gavin Newsom’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. But the office has been critical of the administration’s past efforts. In May, Newsom’s office called the action to withhold funds for in-home care programs a “sick” and politically motivated attack on services that are meant to “keep seniors and people with disabilities OUT of nursing homes.” Those services usually cover assistants who help people with daily tasks such as bathing, laundry or cooking. They also provide needed care such as injections under the direction of a medical professional. A 2020 report by the California state auditor found that nearly three-quarters of In-home Supportive Services caregivers assist a family member. Newsom’s office, however, has argued that the program saves taxpayers money, saying IHSS care costs $30,000 a year, while nursing home care costs $137,000 a year. Read more: Medicaid reckoning awaits next California governor after program’s rapid expansion California’s hospice industry has had problems in the past and authorities have tried to crack down on the issue. A Times investigation in 2020 found that providers were billing Medicare for hospice services and equipment for patients who were not actually dying while the industry boomed. The Trump administration, led by Vice President JD Vance, has tried to focus attention on the issue of waste, fraud and abuse as a centerpiece policy platform to bring down healthcare costs. On Tuesday, Trump and Vance announced a $25-million whistleblower program designed to pay out cash to people who tip off the federal government about fraudsters. The program will offer a 1% commission for tips that lead to a successful conviction. Trump said he would be the sole arbitrator of who gets to keep the money. “I’ll determine whether or not the person is deserving, and I will be very generous believe me. We are not looking to save on that,” Trump said. “I promise you I will be fair.” Trump said the money will be handed out “expeditiously and fairly.” “I promise there is nothing in this for me,” he said. The White House referred comment about the decision to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services. The federal agency did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Get the L.A. Times California Politics newsletter. Deeply reported insights into legislation, politics and policy from Sacramento, Washington and beyond, in your inbox twice per week. articles.title: New details emerge about dad who stopped Oregon school shooter within minutes
articles.summary: More details have emerged about the "hero" bystander who intervened within minutes of a gunman opening fire at an elementary school in Oregon. Kaylub Giamanco, 36, fatally shot the 16-year-old gunman who killed four people at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Ore., on Oct. 15. His actions "undoubtedly saved people," police said. Giamanco, a carpenter and father of two girls who attend Silver Rail Elementary, had gone through "military shooting drills" with veterans who fought in Iraq, The Guardian reported. Seeing the shooting unfold, Giamanco "pursued" gunman Griffin J. John II, his mother, Kenda Freeman, told CBS News . Freeman said the experience has left her son traumatized. "I told him he was a hero, he did what he had to do, and that he did the right thing, and that I was proud of him and that he was a hero and he saved a lot of lives." "Kaylub knew something was not right, so he pulled up onto the grass, grabbed his gun and basically stalked the gunman back into the school," Freeman said. "He crawled through a window that the gunman had shot out. He army crawled through the window." Giamanco, who legally owns and carries his weapon, doesn't wish to speak about the school shooting because he feels "riddled with guilt" for not being able to save more lives, his brother, Kyle Giamanco, told the New York Post . A teacher in the classroom had already thrown her cellphone at John, tackled him and fought him, police said. She was not injured. Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said her actions likely prevented more bloodshed. Giamanco then fired at John multiple times with a legally owned .40-caliber pistol, killing him just before police arrived, officials said. Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek  praised the Bend resident at a press conference, without naming him, saying he "heroically intervened to stop further loss of life." Addressing him directly, she acknowledged the toll it had taken on him. "Your actions carry a heavy emotional burden, and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well." "I don't think we can underestimate or under-appreciate that courage," Krantz said Friday, speaking about the teacher and the man who shot the gunman. "When someone is willing to risk their own life for others, we recognize that. And the quick thinking to … follow someone into the school is incredible, and undoubtedly saved people." Gun used 'purchased as a birthday gift' The gun used by the 16-year-old shooter Griffin J. John II was purchased by his mother as a birthday gift, according to reports. The Maverick 12-gauge shotgun was purchased legally in August 2026 by the mother of the gunman who carried out the shooting, and given to him for recreational use, sources told CBS News . On Friday, two senior law enforcement officials told NBC News that John's mother bought the shotgun and has been cooperating with investigators. The shooter killed Rhoam Summer, a 5-year-old student, and Megan Lambert, a 25-year-old teacher from Bend, along with two other children aged 8 and 11 on Thursday. Police said all of the shots were fired inside a single special needs classroom. In an interview with CNN on Sunday, John's mother said that "there were no warning signs" and wouldn't comment on how her son got access to the gun used in the shooting. Schools remain closed Schools across Bend., Ore., will stay closed Monday and Tuesday as the community mourns four people killed on Thursday, when police say a 16-year-old former student opened fire in a special education classroom. Students return Wednesday on an early-release schedule, and Silver Rail will remain closed until further notice, the Bend Bulletin reported . In a statement, Lambert's family described her as a native central Oregonian who grew up in Bend and had a passion for playing sports, especially volleyball. "Her goal was to be an educator and teach in the school district she loved growing up in," the statement continued.  "Silver Rail was her first job as a teacher. … She loved Silver Rail. This was her dream job. Megan was compassionate and had a huge heart. She always fought for the underdog and those with special needs. She was an incredible sister, daughter, niece and granddaughter. … She was funny and opinionated and she lit up the room." Megan Lambert, 25, a teacher at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Ore., was killed in Thursday's shooting. Bend Police Department Rhoam Summer, 5, was one of three children killed in Thursday's shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Ore. Bend Police Department The shooter was identified as Griffin J. John II. He was a former student at the school who had received special ed services, according to Bend-La Pine School Superintendent Steven Cook. The Confederated Tribes of Siletz Indians confirmed Saturday that John was an enrolled member, NBC News reported . A 7-year-old girl who received lifesaving care at the scene was in serious but stable condition at Oregon Health & Science University, police said. A 54-year-old teacher, Becky Drury of Bend, suffered serious but non-life-threatening injuries and was being treated at St. Charles Bend. Her family allowed police to release her name. Becky Drury, 54, a teacher at Silver Rail Elementary School, was injured in Thursday's shooting. Bend Police Department According to a Facebook post from her mother-in-law, Drury has already had surgery to repair significant damage to her left arm and will need more surgeries in the future. She also suffered injuries to her right hand, but none of her wounds are believed to be life-threatening. "The good news is she will be ok and we all get to keep that magnificent woman we love so much in our lives," the post read. Her husband, Will Drury, said her left arm "took a lot of damage" and that her right hand also needed surgery, CNN reported . The two other children killed, both boys, were 8 and 11. Their families asked police not to release their names. Other than John's past association with the school, police did not share any information on the potential motive behind the shooting. "Everyone wants to know why, including us," Krantz said. "We may never get that full answer, but we want it." How the shooting unfolded Flowers are placed beside a sign at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Ore., on Friday. AP Photo/Haven Daley Krantz provided new details about what happened in the chaotic few minutes from when John first opened fire outside the school to when he was killed. According to Krantz, John approached the school at approximately 12:58 p.m. on foot before throwing his gun over an exterior fence and climbing onto the school's property. A driver in a red pickup truck spotted John and "verbally confronted" him from inside their vehicle. John fired at least three rounds at the truck before heading inside. The driver, who was unhurt, quickly called 911 to alert police. John then walked around the outside of the school and fired multiple rounds into the glass panes of an exterior door to gain access to the school. He then turned left into a special education classroom and immediately began firing. In total, John fired as many as 15 rounds, Krantz said. Officers arrived at the scene within three minutes of the first 911 call. "Seconds later, officers reported the suspect had been shot and killed, possibly by a bystander," police wrote in an incident report on Thursday. Officers then cleared the school, and all students and staff were transported to a nearby church for reunification with families and guardians. According to Krantz, John was carrying an additional 44 rounds of ammunition when he was killed. Police had initially said that the three children who were killed and the one who was injured were the only students in the classroom at the time of the shooting. But on Monday, they confirmed that a fifth student had been present.  That student was "physically unharmed by the assailant," a spokesman for the school district told the Oregonian . A fourth adult, a special education staff member who was also unharmed, was also in the room, police said. Investigators have searched John's home and plan to keep control of the school until at least Tuesday to finish collecting evidence, police said. They are asking anyone with video of a teenage boy in black clothing and a black backpack near Third Street, Brosterhous Road or the school between 10 a.m. and 1 p.m. Thursday to submit it. The FBI has set up a tipline at 1-800-CALL-FBI and fbi.gov/silverrailschool . 'Rhoam was so so strong' People leave a family reunification area following a shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Ore., on Thursday. AP Photo/Joe Kline Rhoam Summer's parents, Kelik and Lillian, released a new statement on Monday through their attorneys providing more details on who he was and how best to honor his memory. "Rhoam was so so strong. The day he was born, his father gave him his first sink bath at the hospital. In the sink, Rhoam grabbed his dad's hands and pulled himself up with his own strength. He climbed a ladder (3 step stool) when he was just 6 months old. He never stopped moving. He never stopped climbing. He could do anything," they wrote in the statement shared by the law firm Dwyer Williams & Cherkoss. A GoFundMe set up by friends of the family, one of 10 fundraisers that the site has verified to support those connected to the shooting, has raised more than $187,000 as of Tuesday. In their statement, the Summers said another way to remember Rhoam is to embody the spirit he lived with. "If people want to memorialize our little Rhoam, we request you draw. Sharks, dinosaurs, monsters... Rhoam loved to tell stories of creatures with big teeth who needed understanding and friendship. Please make art for him. Draw or paint. Use your hands if you can. Get messy," they wrote. Dwyer Williams & Cherkoss is one of three law firms the Summers have reportedly hired to "preserve and protect Rhoam's memory and investigate possible legal claims arising from the mass school shooting," according to the Salem Statesman Journal . "Senseless, barbaric, and depraved? Yes. But was it foreseeable and thus preventable?" Tim Williams, cocounsel on the investigation, told the paper. "That's what we will find out. While law enforcement handles the criminal prosecution, we will be investigating any systemic failures that may have allowed this tragedy to happen. We are committed to holding all responsible parties accountable to ensure a tragedy like this never happens again and justice is done in Rhoam's name." articles.title: Ohio governor candidate hits back after estranged mother appears in attack ad
articles.summary: COLUMBUS, Ohio (AP) — Dr. Amy Acton , the Democratic candidate for Ohio governor who has made no secret of a difficult childhood that included homelessness and sexual abuse, pushed back forcefully Tuesday against an unattributed ad circulating online in which her long-estranged mother calls her “a liar” and insinuates she has mental health issues. The ad began circulating overnight, just two weeks before Election Day. Acton, Ohio's former public health director , is in a tight race with Republican billionaire Vivek Ramaswamy , a 2024 presidential candidate who has benefited from spending on his behalf that has exceeded $120 million. The online ad, which first surfaced in a post by an Ohio political blogger, spread quickly across social media platforms. It does not include the “paid for” tag that is legally required to air on TV so viewers can know who produced and paid for it. D.J. Brynes, who blogs as “The Rooster,” told CNN he got the video from a voter who viewed it as part of a poll and recorded it. It was not clear if Acton's mother was paid for the one-minute spot. Her last known telephone number has been disconnected. Acton suggested Ramaswamy was behind the ad. “I won’t normalize somebody who has said that my childhood is just something I’m complaining about, who today just released an ad using my birth mother, who I was removed from at the age of 12 for severe abuse and neglect, and sexual abuse," she told Spectrum News, a cable news outlet in Ohio. She said Ramaswamy was accused of similar personal attacks during his run for the GOP presidential nomination: “This is a lifelong pattern with my opponent.” Ramaswamy’s campaign issued a statement that did not address if he was responsible for the ad or knew who produced it. In the statement, campaign spokeswoman Connie Luck said Acton “has some serious problems with the truth that the public needs to be aware of.” In a statement released by Acton's campaign, her brother, Philip Stearns, said the two were removed from their mother Donna Arthur's custody as children after their stepfather, Arthur's husband, was indicted for raping Acton as a child. Acton has not seen Arthur, whose last known address was in Pennsylvania, since they were in a courtroom together in 1978. Later Tuesday, the Acton campaign released a response ad featuring Stearns, who recalls his older sister taking “the worst” of the abuse they faced as children in order to protect him and disparages Ramaswamy and his allies for exploiting the situation. According to police and court documents obtained by The Associated Press, Cledith Arthur was arrested and charged with the rape of his stepdaughter, then 12, in July 1978, after Acton's biological father reported his alleged conduct to authorities. The abuse allegedly happened from December 1976 to April 1978. Cledith Arthur pleaded not guilty. He was indicted by a grand jury that September, but failed to show at a court hearing and remained a fugitive until at least 1981. He has since died. High-profile Republicans who back Ramaswamy — including Donald Trump Jr. and influencer Laura Loomer — elevated the video in online posts. But other Republicans joined Democrats in condemning the ad. Meghan McCain called it “dastardly” and Dan Hauser, a strategist for Republican Sen. Mike Lee of Utah, said he deleted his retweet of the ad once he realized “the very serious accusations that caused their issues.” The Democrat running for U.S. Senate in Ohio, Sherrod Brown, described the spot as “disgusting” and said everyone — including his opponent, Sen. Jon Husted — should be willing to condemn it. A spokesperson for Husted's campaign didn't immediately respond to a request for comment. Acton's mother does not mention Ramaswamy's name in the ad, but she suggests that Acton has misrepresented her opponent and the time her family was homeless and living in a tent when she was a child — an experience Stearns corroborates. ___ Associated Press writer Ali Swenson in New York contributed to this report. articles.title: Trump uses antisemitic term in defending a senator at a Kansas rally
articles.summary: President Donald Trump speaks during a campaign rally in Park City, Kansas, a suburb of Wichita, on October 19. - Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty Images President Donald Trump on Monday used an antisemitic term that he has used publicly at least once before as he​ defended Kansas Sen. Roger Marshall against criticism over medical billing practices. Trump invoked the term “Shylock” while defending Marshall’s​ suing more than 700 patients for outstanding medical bills during his time as an obstetrician-gynecologist, as first reported by The New York Times . “You’re not allowed not to do it. You have to, by law, go after those people, and they made it like, oh, he was some kind of a Shylock-type guy,” Trump said at a rally in Kansas. “If he didn’t make these requests, he would be breaking the law. He would have been breaking a very strong criminal law, and he would be subject to criminal arrest and liability.” (That underlying claim is not true, according to Lawrence Gostin , faculty director of the O’Neill Institute for National and Global Health Law at Georgetown Law School: “He’s entitled to sue for unpaid bills but not required to do so.”) Trump has previously faced criticism for using the term.​ In July 2025 , he  said it during a rally in Iowa. He later claimed he didn’t know the word was viewed by some as antisemitic. “I’ve never heard it that way. To me, Shylock is somebody that’s a money lender at high rates,” Trump told reporters at the time. “I’ve never heard it that way, you view it differently than me. I’ve never heard that.” The Anti-Defamation League — which last year condemned Trump’s use of the word — wrote Tuesday on X that the term was “rooted in a longstanding antisemitic stereotype.” “Regardless of intent, its use can reinforce harmful tropes about Jews and normalize language that has long been used to target the Jewish community,” the group wrote. Amy Spitalnick, CEO of the Jewish Council for Public Affairs, noted on X that Trump had previously been criticized publicly for using the term. “Tonight Trump yet again used the antisemitic ‘Shylock’ — a year after he was called out for doing so and claimed he didn’t know it was problematic,” she said. “Again: not an accident. He has consistently normalized antisemitic conspiracy theories and tropes.” In 2014 , former President Joe Biden apologized for using the word. articles.title: 'Jane Doe' says Cornell president questioned why she waited to report rape allegations
articles.summary: The former Cornell student who alleges she was drugged and raped by seven members of a fraternity on the school's Ithaca, N.Y., campus in October 2024, wrote in a letter to faculty leadership that the university’s president expressed doubt in her account months after she reported it to campus police. In a two-page letter to the Faculty Senate obtained by the New York Times , the former student, identified in a civil lawsuit as "Jane Doe," said that Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff’s “initial response” to her allegations “was along the lines of, ‘Why did she wait so long to report it?’” The alleged assault occurred at the Chi Phi fraternity house on Oct. 19 and 20, 2024. She reported it to campus police on Nov. 8. Read more from Yahoo: A timeline of the Cornell University rape case According to Jane Doe, Kotlikoff’s response came during a private meeting he had in January 2025 with leaders of Cornell’s sororities — including hers. She said the sorority president then relayed the comments to her. “I felt unsupported and disbelieved by President Kotlikoff,” the former student wrote in her letter to the Faculty Senate. “It diminished my confidence in the administration’s ability to approach my experience with the understanding, sensitivity, and fairness I had hoped for and expected from what had been my dream school.” In a statement to the Times, Cornell said that the “second-hand account” of the president’s exchange was inaccurate and that his comments were not directed at Jane Doe. “The question ‘Why did it take so long for the assault to be reported?’ was directed at bystanders who did not use Cornell’s anonymous tip line, despite ongoing social media activity about the incident in October 2024,” the university said in a statement. “He was not questioning Jane Doe’s reporting.” Cornell students participate in a campus rally on Oct. 5 protesting the university's handling of the "Jane Doe" case. Spencer Platt/Getty Images Cornell’s handling of the Jane Doe case has come under intense scrutiny, reigniting the national debate over consent and sexual assault on college campuses and triggering calls for Kotlikoff to resign. The Faculty Senate is considering a no-confidence resolution to condemn the school's response to sexual violence on campus. A vote on the resolution is expected at the end of the month. In an interview with the New York Times last week , Kotlikoff said he learned of Jane Doe's allegations shortly after she reported them to campus police, but did not follow up with her or seek to determine whether the fraternity members she accused had been punished. He also said he was not informed when Matthew Van Houten, the local prosecutor, declined to bring charges and that he was unaware Jane Doe had dropped out of Cornell until last month, when she filed suit. "The fact that Jane Doe experienced what she experienced at Cornell is something that I am personally sorry for," Kotlikoff said. "And I think this entire campus is sorry that occurred." All of the men identified in Jane Doe's civil suit have denied any wrongdoing, and none has been charged with a crime. articles.title: 光缆集采单价疯涨300%！AI加持下的光纤超级周期还能走多久？
articles.summary: 中国电信一笔109亿元的光缆集采，折射出全球光纤产业的价格变化：传统运营商采购量增长有限，光纤报价却显著抬升。AI数据中心带来的新需求、光棒与高性能光纤的制造约束，正在改变持续多年的低价竞争格局。 2027年供给偏紧仍有支撑，2028年前后新增产能将逐步检验涨价的持续性。普通光纤与高性能产品的盈利走势可能分化，企业的成本能力、订单结构和资本开支纪律将决定最终利润归属。 一、发生了什么？——中国电信109亿元订单确认接受光纤涨价 1．17家企业同价竞标，运营商采购出现了什么变化？ 10月15日，中国电信2026—2027年室外光缆集中采购项目披露中标候选人，18家企业入围，其中17家的含税投标总价均为109.04亿元，仅有一家略低。如此整齐的报价，在过去习惯以低价争夺运营商订单的光纤行业格外引人注目。 行业媒体披露本轮采购规模约8000万芯公里，对照上一轮约7500万芯公里、约25亿元的市场估计，数量增幅只有约6.7%，金额却增长逾三倍。按相同方式粗略折算，每芯公里金额由约33元升至约136元。差异主要来自价格，不过采购周期、产品规格及数量构成尚未完全统一，不能把折算结果当作某一款裸纤的实际成交单价。运营商的采购限价明显抬升，表明其已经将持续涨价纳入工程成本安排。 另一个值得注意的细节是长协价格与现货价格之间的差距。行业材料援引第三方估算，本轮集采所隐含的裸纤基准约81元/芯公里，低于同期约105—110元的散纤报价。这个差额提示出长协的商业逻辑：运营商以采购稳定性交换价格折让，上游厂商则以确定的订单覆盖未来产量。若现货继续上涨，锁价会限制一部分收益；若行情降温，长协又能保护产能利用率和现金流。 2．普通光纤涨了数倍，高端产品涨得更快： 价格上涨已经超出单个招标项目的范围。TrendForce于10月19日发布的预测显示，2026年G.652.D主流单模光纤现货均价有望由2025年的18元升至85元/芯公里；G.654.E低损耗光纤由45元升至170元；G.657.A2抗弯光纤由33元升至200元。对应涨幅约为372%、278%和506%。年度均价预测呈现价格中枢的变化，即时现货报价则反映阶段性供需紧张。 ……

articles.summary: 美国国家情报总监兼人工智能事务主管Jay Clayton表示，AI工作组有关负责任开发AI的建议将“很快”公布。 周二，Clayton在接受CNBC采访时，被问及何时会提出有关AI的建议，他表示：“我们会陆续提出”，不过他补充称，无法承诺一个确切的日期。 10月16日，特朗普政府新设的AI特别工作组召开首次会议，确立运作框架，并启动多项具体工作机制。该工作组正式运作期限为120天。 工作组由Jay Clayton牵头，核心成员还包括人事管理局局长Scott Kupor、联邦贸易委员会主席Andrew Ferguson，以及国防部技术负责人Emil Michael。 在首次会议上，工作组确立了三个专项委员会的职责划分：报告与响应委员会由Michael主导，关键基础设施委员会由Kupor负责，执法与责任委员会则由Ferguson领衔。 此外，AI对劳动力及经济影响的相关报告将提交劳工部。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 美企起诉特朗普对加拿大征收50%关税，援引大萧条时代法律遭质疑
articles.summary: 新泽西食品进口商Gellert Global Group周二对特朗普政府提起诉讼，挑战其依据一部近百年前立法对加拿大商品征收50%关税的合法性。 这是继最高法院今年2月推翻特朗普"对等关税"之后，同一法律团队发起的又一轮司法攻势。 诉讼由自由正义中心（Liberty Justice Center）代理提交至美国国际贸易法院，要求法院宣告相关关税违法、叫停执行，并责令特朗普政府退还已缴纳税款及利息。 被诉关税自8月22日起正式生效，适用于加拿大曲棍球棒、葡萄酒、蜂蜜、假发及奶酪等多类商品。 此案的背后是更广泛的贸易政策不确定性。自由正义中心此前成功在最高法院推翻特朗普"对等关税"，迫使联邦政府退还估计约1660亿美元的已征税款，目前该机构还有另外两起针对特朗普关税措施的诉讼正在进行中。 争议焦点：一部从未被动用过的大萧条时代法律 特朗普于7月20日签署三份总统公告，援引1930年《关税法》第338条，以加拿大在汽车、酒类及乳制品领域存在所谓不公平贸易待遇为由，对特定加拿大商品征收50%关税。 这部法律颁布96年来从未被实际使用过，如今是第一次被援引来征税。 诉状还主张，就算该法律依然有效，特朗普政府加征关税也不符合法定条件。 因为按照该条款，总统不能随心所欲动用关税，必须先查实外国确实对美国产品实施了歧视性收费或贸易限制； 此外，关税额度也只能用来“弥补损失”，而不能搞无上限的惩罚。 诉状还强调，特朗普所谓的加拿大“歧视性”行为并不属实。 一方面 ，其中两项行为只是加拿大对美国先前关税的反制措施，“反制报复不能算作歧视”，况且美国的对等关税此前已被最高法院判定违法。 另一方面 ，关于乳制品配额的争议源于《美墨加协定》的谈判约定，该条款实际上给了美国奶酪进入加拿大市场极大的优惠待遇，远优于其他绝大多数国家。 原告损失测算，年缴税款估计达4000万美元 作为原告的Gellert Global Group年营收逾17亿美元。诉状披露，该公司2025年进口了价值7100万美元的加拿大奶酪，品类涵盖羊奶酪、山羊奶酪、马斯卡彭、布里干酪、卡芒贝尔及混合奶酪borgonzola等。 在《美墨加协定》框架下，该公司此前对所有加拿大奶酪进口均免缴关税。但随着50%关税生效，Gellert测算其每年须额外承担约4000万美元的税款负担。 公司表示，计划在今年年底前通过内部消化吸收相关成本，但这一状况"长期不可持续"。 诉状警告，若关税持续，公司将被迫提价，导致销售下滑、客户流失、货架陈列风险上升，并可能因供应商成本压力引发供应链中断。 特朗普政府7月已表示，不会续签《美墨加协定》另一个16年任期，这进一步加剧了企业对未来贸易环境的不确定性预期。 司法施压持续，白宫暂未回应 自由正义中心首席执行官Sara Albrecht在声明中表示： 案并非针对总统个人，而是关乎总统权力的边界。任何一位总统，都不应该拥有随意激活一部‘休眠’已久的旧法、进而绕过国会限制去征收巨额关税或下达进口禁令的特权。 截至发稿，白宫尚未就诉讼置评。加拿大此前已对美国商品实施"等额"报复性关税。对等关税被推翻后，联邦政府已启动退款程序，预计退款规模约1660亿美元。 目前，自由正义中心在对等关税之外，仍有另外两起针对特朗普关税措施的诉讼在审，这意味着特朗普政府在贸易政策上面临的司法压力短期内难以消退。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 特朗普中选后打击伊朗筹码？美第三艘航母据称料11月底抵中东、增派约万人
articles.summary: 美国正进一步加强在中东的军事部署。据美媒消息，“罗斯福”号航空母舰打击群与第13海军陆战队远征部队预计于11月底抵达中东，相当于增派约1万名海军官兵及海军陆战队员；此次部署将为特朗普政府提供更多军事选项，而特朗普正在考虑于11月中期选举后加大对伊朗的军事打击。 此次增兵将涉及航母打击群、两栖戒备群及海军陆战队远征部队。若“罗斯福”号抵达时“华盛顿”号仍留在中东，美国在该地区的航母部署规模将暂时增至三艘。不过，相关部署也可能涉及现有舰艇的轮换，三艘航母是否会同时留驻仍有变数。 这并非美国首次披露向中东增派第三艘航母的计划。 10月初，新华社曾援引《华尔街日报》报道称，美国国防部正向中东派遣第三个航空母舰打击群和更多海军陆战队舰艇，还向该地区增派近1万名士兵。当时报道提到，美国官员表示，舰艇、战斗机和海军陆战队员将于11月底抵达中东地区。 最新消息则进一步明确了此次部署的具体兵力构成，并再次将其与特朗普可能在中期选举后对伊朗采取更大规模军事行动的考量联系起来。 “罗斯福”号航母打击群与海军陆战队同步部署 根据福克斯新闻记者Liz Friden于美东时间20日周二的报道，两名美国官员证实，美国正向中东派遣“罗斯福”号航母打击群，以及第13海军陆战队远征部队。相关舰艇及人员预计最迟于11月底抵达。 其中，“罗斯福”号航母打击群约有6000名水兵；第13海军陆战队远征部队则随“马金岛”号两栖戒备群部署，后者通常包括约4200名海军陆战队员和水兵。此次部署预计为中东增加约1万名海军及海军陆战队人员。 “罗斯福”号航母打击群此次从美国圣迭戈出发，随后经日本横须贺基地短暂停留，再继续驶向中东。“马金岛”号两栖戒备群也将与海军陆战队远征部队协同行动。 航母打击群主要提供舰载航空作战能力与海上控制能力；两栖戒备群及海军陆战队远征部队则能够提供两栖作战、空中支援及快速部署地面兵力等选项。两类力量同步部署，将使美国在中东拥有更为多样的军事行动能力。 中东现有两艘航母，第三艘能否同时驻留仍存变数 目前，美国在中东已有“乔治·H·W·布什”号和“乔治·华盛顿”号两艘航母部署。“布什”号于今年4月抵达该地区，“华盛顿”号则于8月中旬抵达，接替此前部署的“亚伯拉罕·林肯”号。 如果“罗斯福”号抵达后，“华盛顿”号仍继续留在中东，美国将自今年4月以来再次在该地区同时部署三个航母打击群。但《华尔街日报》此前报道也指出，“华盛顿”号可能在“罗斯福”号抵达后离开中东，返回其位于日本的母港，因此不能将三艘航母同时驻留视为已经确定的安排。 除航母打击群外，美国还在中东部署了“拳师”号两栖戒备群的部分舰艇。 据新华社援引《华尔街日报》10月1日的报道，当时美国官员预计，在新增兵力抵达后，该地区美军总人数将超过5万人。 新一轮部署意味着美军将进一步增强在该地区的军事存在，但同时也会增加航母及相关作战力量的部署压力。 特朗普考虑中期选举后扩大对伊军事行动 此次增兵的关键背景，是特朗普政府正在考虑下一阶段对伊朗的军事选项。 《华尔街日报》10月初报道称，特朗普正在考虑于11月中期选举后恢复对伊朗的轰炸行动。福克斯新闻10月20日的最新报道同样指出，新一轮军事部署将为美国提供更多选择，以便特朗普政府在考虑后续行动时拥有更强的军事能力。不过，现有报道并不意味着白宫已经作出发动新一轮大规模打击的最终决定。 地区局势仍面临多重不确定性。新华社此前报道，美国与伊朗围绕霍尔木兹海峡通行安排等问题存在分歧，特朗普曾表示，伊朗提出的重新开放海峡方案“不够好”。海峡安全、对伊军事行动及相关谈判的进展，都可能影响美国后续的军事部署和决策。 从10月初披露派遣第三艘航母和增派近万名军人，到最新消息再次确认部署安排并预计11月底抵达，美国正在为中东局势可能进一步升级预留更多军事选项。接下来，关键观察点将是三艘航母能否同时留驻、增援部队的实际抵达时间，以及特朗普是否会在中期选举后将军事部署转化为新一轮对伊打击行动。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 瑞士9月黄金出口额环比增长6%，对英出口创2012年以来新高
articles.summary: 瑞士9月黄金出口量升至2025年2月以来最高水平，对英国出口更创至少2012年以来的单月新高。英国黄金市场资金流入增加，成为推动瑞士黄金出口增长的重要因素。 瑞士海关数据显示，9月瑞士黄金出口量环比增长6%，达到165.2吨。其中，对英国出口量环比增长24%，达到126.2吨。 瑞士是全球主要的黄金精炼和转运中心之一，英国则拥有全球最大的场外黄金交易市场，两地之间的黄金流动受到投资需求、交易活动及库存配置等因素影响。 9月对主要黄金消费国印度的出口环比下降12%，至3.1吨。上周印度黄金交易价格时隔三个多月首次出现溢价，金价回落提振了珠宝购买需求。 周二，黄金现货下跌0.4%，自8月25日阶段性高点以来，已下跌12%。 英国黄金投资需求走强 英国黄金流入增加之际，黄金ETF投资需求也保持强劲。 世界黄金协会数据显示，2026年第三季度，全球实物支持型黄金ETF净流入创纪录的310亿美元。 其中，英国上市黄金ETF吸引约75亿美元资金流入，创下单季最高纪录。9月，全球黄金ETF净流入约100亿美元，持仓增加67吨，达到4256吨的历史新高。 世界黄金协会指出，英国上市黄金ETF在截至9月25日的13周中有12周录得资金流入。 近期恰逢英国国债期限溢价上升，英国上市黄金ETF资金持续流入可能反映出投资者对通胀不确定性、财政可持续性和主权债券市场风险的普遍担忧 。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 美伊谈判突破传言搅动市场，妥协方案浮出水面但以色列进入最高战备，分析人士称新战事概率达90%
articles.summary: 新近消息显示，外交斡旋与军事备战正在中东同步提速。卡塔尔与巴基斯坦联合提出的妥协方案令市场短暂燃起和平希望，但伊朗官员的强硬表态、以色列军队进入最高战备状态，以及美国防长赫格塞思访以共同勾勒出一幅外交与冲突赛跑的紧张图景。分析人士警告，美伊爆发第三轮大规模战争的概率已高达90%。 10月20日周二，卡塔尔媒体获悉，卡塔尔与巴基斯坦向美国和伊朗提交了一份妥协提案，并获美伊初步认可。彭博社提到，一则未经证实的报道称，旨在达成协议、结束美伊战事的谈判最快本周就可能取得突破。消息一出，国际原油期货盘中转跌，美油和布油日内跌幅均曾扩大至约3.3%，布油曾跌至106美元/桶下方；三大美股指集体上行。 然而不到一小时后，据彭博援引参与谈判的外交官消息，伊朗与美国的谈判仍在继续，但“即将达成协议”的说法不属实。原油加速收窄跌幅，布油曾重上109.30美元、日内跌不足0.2%，美油一度跌不到0.6%。 与此同时，以色列国防军总参谋长、陆军中将Eyal Zamir宣布军队进入“最高战备状态”并取消士兵休假，美国防长赫格塞思秘密到访以色列南部奥夫达空军基地与内塔尼亚胡举行密谈，进一步加剧了外界对军事行动迫在眉睫的担忧。 卡塔尔媒体称妥协方案推动美伊恢复谈判 美媒称即将达成协议报道不实 据与卡塔尔外交政策立场较为接近的媒体Al-Araby Al-Jadeed援引“熟悉调解努力的知情人士”报道，卡塔尔与巴基斯坦联合提出了一份“中间妥协提案”。巴基斯坦陆军参谋长、陆军元帅穆尼尔10月20日亲赴德黑兰，将该提案提交给伊朗高级官员。 据报道，该提案的核心内容包括两个方面：其一，国际原子能机构（IAEA）对伊朗核设施进行非公开的私下检查，以回应美方在核问题上的核心诉求；其二，将伊朗存放于卡塔尔银行的60亿美元冻结资金所产生的利息转交伊朗，部分满足伊朗要求返还冻结资产的诉求。提案目标是防止冲突再度升级，为双方重返谈判桌创造条件。 然而，周二美股早盘尾声时，美媒彭博社援引参与谈判的外交官表示，有关双方即将达成协议的报道不属实，谈判仍在进行中，尚未触及最终协议阶段。 据央视新闻，卡塔尔首相顾问兼外交部发言人马吉德·安萨里周二在多哈举行的第八届全球安全论坛上表示，尽管中东地区紧张局势持续升级，美国与伊朗围绕伊朗核问题的谈判仍在继续，双方均保持外交接触。 安萨里表示，外界缺乏有关谈判进展的公开信息，并不意味着谈判陷入停滞。他指出，闭门外交有助于提高斡旋成功的可能性，相关进展未被公开，可能恰恰说明调解工作正在有效推进。 安萨里强调，卡塔尔将继续发挥外交斡旋作用，借鉴以往调解经验，应对不同冲突带来的挑战，推动通过对话和外交途径解决地区争端。 伊朗强硬表态，核材料去留成核心障碍 妥协方案传出的同一天，伊朗官员发出了一系列强硬信号，令外界对谈判前景的乐观预期大打折扣。 据央视新闻，伊朗最高国家安全委员会秘书雷扎伊在会见穆尼尔时强调，所有浓缩核材料都将留在伊朗，这些材料是伊朗人民的宝贵财富，将在国内使用。 雷扎伊称，伊朗全体人民和官员一致认为，在美方建立信任之前，不会进行任何谈判。而建立信任的第一步，就是满足伊朗提出的条件。 另据央视，伊朗议会议长卡利巴夫在会见穆尼尔时亦表示，美国长期以来对伊朗的负面行动，使伊朗对美国极度不信任。如今，特朗普政府违反了《伊斯兰堡谅解备忘录》，一再的威胁更加剧了这种不信任。美国若不履行伊朗提出的七项条件，便无法赢得伊朗的信任。军事威胁和行动不能影响伊朗的战略决策。正是美国误判形势，发动对伊朗的战争，才使其陷入泥潭，现在他们必须采取必要措施脱身。 美国外交政策智库Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft的联合创始人兼执行副总Trita Parsi指出，美国坚持要求伊朗将60%浓缩铀提前运出境外，作为谈判前提，而伊朗对此明确拒绝，这一根本分歧使任何综合性协议都难以落地。 Parsi表示：“伊朗主要寻求临时性协议以降低眼前紧张态势，而不会在特朗普离任前认真处理核心核问题。” 以色列进入最高战备，美防长秘访以引发战事升级猜测 军事层面的动作同样令市场神经紧绷。以色列国防军总参谋长Eyal Zamir周一召集高级军官举行评估会议，宣布军队进入“最高战备状态”并取消士兵休假，官方理由是确保10月27日以色列议会选举安全顺利进行。 Zamir表示，以色列国防军“处于最高战备状态，将在未来一段时间内继续在所有战线保持高度警惕和战备水平”。值得注意的是，以色列媒体和官员均未援引任何具体威胁或挑衅行为作为提升战备级别的直接原因。 据央视新闻，以色列总理发言人证实，内塔尼亚胡此前一天在以色列南部奥夫达空军基地会见了到访的美国国防部长赫格塞思，双方就应对伊朗等中东安全局势举行了未公开的秘密会晤。该基地驻扎有美军战斗机和加油机。以色列总理办公室、美国国防部和以色列驻美大使馆均未就此置评。 就上述消息，以色列总理办公室、美国国防部和以色列驻美大使馆均未予置评。赫格塞思此前仅证实其前往中东地区进行了未公开行程并视察了美军部队，未明确说明具体地点。 央视提到，另有消息称，以色列空军近期出动10架战斗机从内瓦提姆空军基地起飞，越过叙利亚并进入伊拉克领空进行多次模拟打击演练，旨在维持对伊朗防空系统的威慑压力，并模糊训练与实际行动之间的界限，但以军方未予证实。 Trita Parsi综合上述信号判断，“特朗普与内塔尼亚胡的协调配合、赫格塞思的突然到访、部队调动，以及最重要的——一份对伊朗而言根本无法接受的美方提案，使第三轮战争爆发的可能性在我的评估中已达到90%”，并警告冲突可能在美国中期选举前、甚至以色列大选前就已爆发。 伊朗拖延策略与胡塞武装联动，地区风险叠加 据路透援引三名伊朗高级官员及一名伊朗内部人士的匿名表述，伊朗蓄意拖延与美国的间接谈判，意图在政治上削弱特朗普，为11月美国中期选举制造压力。其中一名官员表示，“伊朗正在为美以重新发动攻击做准备，而非准备与美国达成协议结束战争”，伊朗政府“决心不给特朗普政治上的胜利。” 德黑兰分析人士Saeed Leylaz向路透表示，伊朗通过拖延基本毫无进展的间接谈判，“在不采取任何违法行动的情况下影响美国选举”。 与此同时，地区局势的联动效应正在加剧整体风险。 据报道，伊朗在霍尔木兹海峡持续对国际航运发动袭击，本月已创下历史纪录频次，但美军迄今未予直接反击。在阿拉伯半岛，胡塞武装近期加大了对沙特阿拉伯的弹道导弹打击力度，这一态势有可能将波斯湾与也门两个冲突战场连为一体，进一步压缩外交斡旋空间。
